annotations.title: Symptoms & Causes of Urinary Retention - NIDDK

content.text:
A bladder that doesn’t empty fully is called **urinary retention**. It usually happens for one of two broad reasons: **something is blocking urine flow**, or **the bladder muscle/nerves aren’t working well enough to push urine out**. ([niddk.nih.gov](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/urologic-diseases/urinary-retention.?utm_source=openai))

Common causes include:

- **Enlarged prostate** in men, which can squeeze the urethra and slow/block urine flow.
- **Urinary tract infection (UTI)** or inflammation causing swelling and difficulty urinating.
- **Constipation**, which can press on the bladder/urethra.
- **Certain medications**, especially some cold/allergy meds, decongestants, antihistamines, antidepressants, opioids, muscle relaxers, and some bladder medications.
- **Nerve problems** from diabetes, spinal cord issues, multiple sclerosis, stroke, Parkinson’s disease, or pelvic surgery/injury.
- **Weak or underactive bladder muscle**, where the bladder doesn’t squeeze strongly enough.
- **Urethral stricture/scarring**, bladder stones, or tumors blocking flow.
- **After surgery/anesthesia**, which can temporarily impair bladder function.
- In women: **pelvic organ prolapse**, prior pelvic surgery, pregnancy/postpartum changes, or pelvic masses can contribute.

**Seek urgent care now** if you **cannot urinate at all**, have severe lower belly pain/pressure, fever, back/flank pain, vomiting, new leg weakness/numbness, or blood in the urine—acute urinary retention can become an emergency. ([niddk.nih.gov](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/urologic-diseases/urinary-retention/symptoms-causes?utm_source=openai))

If this is ongoing but you can still urinate, it’s still worth seeing a clinician/urologist. They can check a urine test, kidney function, and do a **bladder scan after you pee** to see how much urine is left.
